query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Cryogenic deformation (e.g., cryo-rolling) followed by controlled annealing transforms the conventional lamellar structure into a refined, hierarchical nano-lamellar microstructure with enhanced phase boundary integrity, thereby simultaneously increasing both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility in eutectic HEAs.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase (L12 and B2) lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation, resulting in brittle behavior at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Apply cryogenic deformation (cryo-rolling) followed by an optimized annealing treatment.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation; starting with an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 or similar eutectic HEA featuring dual-phase lamellar colonies.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, hierarchical nano-lamellar structure characterized by fine lamellar regions with ultrafine grains and well-bonded phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Cryogenic deformation enhances strain partitioning and refines the microstructure, while subsequent annealing promotes recovery and recrystallization in a controlled way. The resulting hierarchical microstructure reduces stress concentrations at internal boundaries, mitigating microcrack formation and enabling an improved balance of strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified lamellar baseline, the treated alloy will show a significant increase in yield and ultimate tensile strength along with increased elongation to failure (ductility), effectively overcoming the classical strength-ductility trade-off.
generation.baseline: Conventional as-cast or cold-rolled and annealed eutectic HEAs with coarser lamellar colonies and lower tensile ductility.
generation.boundary: The effect is limited to eutectic HEAs with a lamellar (L12 + B2) dual-phase structure and may not be effective for alloys with substantially different compositions or phase distributions. Optimization of cryo-deformation parameters and annealing conditions is critical.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal processing parameters (degree of cryo-rolling reduction and annealing temperature/time) and the detailed evolution of phase boundary characteristics under these treatments remain to be clarified, as does the robustness of the approach across slight compositional variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one using conventional processing (as-cast or cold-rolled and annealed) and the other applying cryogenic deformation followed by controlled annealing. Characterize the microstructure (using SEM/TEM) to assess lamellar refinement and phase boundary quality, and conduct room-temperature tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Grain size distribution and phase boundary integrity via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryo-deformed and annealed samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both strength (YS and UTS) and ductility (elongation to failure) compared to the conventional processing baseline, or if the microstructural analysis does not reveal the expected hierarchical, refined lamellar structure with better phase boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. ## Abstract
Eutectic high entropy alloys, with lamellar arrangement of solid solution phases, represent a new paradigm for simultaneously achieving high strength and ductility, thereby circumventing this well-known trade-off in conventional alloys. However, dynamic strengthening mechanisms and phase-boundary interactions during external loading remain unclear for these eutectic systems. In this study, small-scale mechanical behavior was evaluated for AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy, consisting of a lamellar arrangement of L12 and B2 solid-solution phases. The ultimate tensile strength was 1165 MPa with ductility of ~18% and ultimate compressive strength was 1863 MPa with a total compressive fracture strain of ~34%. Dual mode fracture was observed with ductile failure for L12 phase and brittle mode for B2 phase. Phase-specific mechanical tests using nano-indentation and micro-pillar compression showed higher hardness and strength and larger strain rate sensitivity for B2 compared with L12.
